clue.text: Little beast circling ready-to-mate female entering fold

indicators.note: going round and coming back the other way, so the phrase for being on heat is read backwards

parts.note: an animal ready to mate is in rut

indicators.note: the female's letter goes into the word for fold

parts.note: a ply is a fold or layer, as in two-ply

explanation.surface: A tiny animal goes round a female in season who is getting into a sheep pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little beast' hints at a mammal, but this is a beetle. 'circling' turns IN RUT round to TURNI; 'entering' puts F inside PLY, giving PFLY.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small beetle pest of brassica crops, so a little beast in the insect sense.

clue.text: Spot-kick converted following United defender's initial trip

indicators.note: the penalty comes after the letter for United

parts.note: U is the usual abbreviation for United in football team names
a penalty taken from the spot is called a pen in football slang

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word defender's is used

explanation.surface: A penalty is scored after a United defender trips an opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: The football picture makes 'trip' look like the foul, but it is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To trip someone is to tip them over, so the two verbs are synonyms for knocking a person off their feet.

clue.text: Would others consider us mad covering nether regions?

definitions.text: Would others consider us mad covering nether regions?

indicators.note: the word for mad is wrapped around the underworld's name

parts.note: nuts is slang for mad
Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, so a name for the nether regions

explanation.surface: Naturists wonder whether others think them crazy for covering up their private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: the whole clue is both the wordplay and a wry definition. 'nether regions' looks anatomical but is Dis, the classical underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturists, who go without clothes, might well suppose clothed people think them crazy, which is how the whole clue describes them.

clue.text: One of the items in the fruit bowl going for a song?

definitions.text: One of the items in the fruit bowl going for a song?

parts.words: One of the items in the fruit bowl going for a song
parts.note: a fruit read as ..., a penny each, which is the price of something going for a song

explanation.surface: A cheap piece of fruit in the bowl, sold for next to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the fruit as P EACH: P is a penny, so the items cost a penny each, which is 'going for a song', meaning very cheap.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone fruit commonly kept in a fruit bowl, and its name splits into a cheap price.

clue.text: Scottish lover's raising the pulse

indicators.note: in a down answer, raising the word lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: dal is a pulse, lentils or split peas, as used in Indian cooking

explanation.surface: A Scottish sweetheart's heart rate goes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulse' suggests a heartbeat, but it is the edible seed, dal. In Scots a lad is a young man or boyfriend.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots usage the word is used for a young man courting, a sweetheart.

clue.text: Well done ham's second-rate?

definitions.meaning: a cry of applause for a good performance
a radio ham spells the letter B, meaning second-rate (B-grade), with this word from the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Praise for an actor, or a sneer that the ham actor is mediocre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ham' looks like a bad actor but is a radio amateur, who uses the NATO phonetic alphabet; B is the grade for second-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of approval shouted at the end of a performance, the same as saying well done.

clue.text: Lofty breeding-place's fine, stopping eggs dropping onto track

indicators.note: in a down answer, the first part falls on top of the railway letters below it
the word for fine plugs the middle of the word for fish eggs

parts.note: roe is the mass of eggs in a fish
OK means fine or all right
RY is an abbreviation for railway, a track

explanation.surface: A high nesting site is fine as long as eggs don't fall onto a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'breeding-place's' stands for 'is' and is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Rooks nest high in treetops in colonies, so their colony is a breeding site up in the air.

clue.text: Parisian is going to nurse one through

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the French verb wraps around the numeral

parts.note: va is French for 'is going', from aller, to go
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A woman from Paris is about to look after someone through an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parisian' signals French: il va, he goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The preposition means by way of, as in travelling to Rome by way of Paris.

clue.text: Decisive uprising of people supporting company vocally

indicators.note: in a down answer the lower part holds up the upper one
spoken out loud, so a word that sounds like a ship's company is used

parts.note: a crew is a ship's company

indicators.note: in a down answer, rising means the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: laic means of the people, the laity rather than clergy

explanation.surface: A popular revolt with spoken backing from a firm turns out to be the decisive moment.
explanation.walkthrough: CRU is a French wine term for a vineyard; it sounds like crew. 'uprising of' turns LAIC to CIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A decisive moment is a critical, all-important one; the words are near synonyms.

clue.text: Went to do some gardening

definitions.meaning: past tense of 'wee', to urinate, as in went to the toilet
to pull up unwanted plants from a flower bed

explanation.surface: Somebody left in order to work in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' looks like plain going, but in the sense of went to the loo it is the past tense of the childish word for urinate.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling out unwanted plants is a basic gardening chore, and the toilet sense is a past tense of a nursery word.

clue.text: Law refreshed with a modern equal-op Lord Mayor in waiting?

indicators.note: the letters are given a fresh new arrangement

explanation.surface: Updated legislation with a new equal-opportunities angle about who could become the next Lord Mayor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'equal-op' are link words; 'equal-op' hints that the alderman of old may now be a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: In the City of London the Lord Mayor is chosen from the aldermen, so a female one is a potential future mayor.

clue.text: Chance of taking such slices from tea — Viennese? No — or maybe yes?

definitions.text: Chance of taking such slices from tea — Viennese? No — or maybe yes?

parts.words: Chance of taking such slices from tea — Viennese? No — or maybe yes
parts.note: the even letters of tea Viennese spell EVENS, a betting price; taking the uneven ones instead gives nothing, so no, then yes

explanation.surface: A puzzled reflection on whether one might get pastries from a Viennese tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of 'tEa ViEnNeSe' and you get EVENS, which is a betting price: the answer, the word for such prices, also means chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting prices express the likelihood of an outcome, so the plural word stands for chance or probability.

clue.text: Pecorino? Che sfortuna!

definitions.meaning: pecorino is a firm Italian sheep's milk cheese, an example hence the question mark
Italian for 'what bad luck!', the British expression of mock sympathy

explanation.surface: An Italian grumbles about bad luck over a piece of pecorino.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are Italian: one a firm cheese, the other an exclamation. 'Hard cheese!' is British slang for tough luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Pecorino is a firm grating cheese, and the British phrase is an unsympathetic way of saying tough luck.

clue.text: During year in navy, discover green grass of Australia

indicators.note: the year with its contents goes inside the navy letters

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy

indicators.note: the environmental word sits within the year letters

parts.note: eco is a prefix meaning green, environmentally friendly

explanation.surface: A sailor discovers green grasslands in Australia during a year with the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green' looks like the grass's colour but is the environmental prefix. 'discover' is only a link; 'During' and 'in' are the two containers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia the cereal rye is commonly called by this two-word name, so it is a grass grown there.

clue.text: The land of Solomon's regal visitor, and man born in it

definitions.text: The land of Solomon's regal visitor

indicators.note: the man and birth letters go inside the word for sex appeal

parts.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
he is a pronoun for a man
B is the abbreviation for born, as in biographies

explanation.surface: A biblical kingdom whose queen visited Solomon, with a man born there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' means sex appeal, SA, as in the 1920s 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible the Queen of Sheba journeyed to visit King Solomon, so her kingdom is the land named.

clue.text: As overbearing type says, so blatantly covering back

indicators.note: the letters are read from right to left
the run of words holds the letters inside it

explanation.surface: A domineering person blatantly agrees with what they say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' and 'type says' read as surface; the letters sit backwards in 'saYS SO Blatantly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone domineering and fond of giving orders is described with this word, a synonym.

clue.text: Wild-cat, one of several in a pound

definitions.meaning: the snow leopard, a big cat of Central Asian mountains

definitions.text: one of several in a pound
definitions.meaning: a pound weight holds sixteen of these units

explanation.surface: A feral cat is one of many in an animal pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pound' suggests a dog pound but is the weight.
explanation.definitionFit: This is another name for the snow leopard, and also a sixteenth of an imperial pound.

clue.text: Lots of storage bays meet minimal requirement of grandee when moving

indicators.note: the letters move around into a new order
just the smallest part, the opening letter, of grandee

explanation.surface: Plenty of storage bays satisfy the basic needs of a nobleman moving house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minimal requirement of grandee' is just G, shuffled in with BAYS MEET.
explanation.definitionFit: Computer memory is measured in millions of bytes, so large amounts of storage are counted in these units.

clue.text: It's a job for me to stick to soulless exercise (it bores)

indicators.note: the second part drills into the word for stick

parts.note: to cling is to stick fast

indicators.note: the heart, the middle letter, is removed

parts.note: to exercise a right is to use it

explanation.surface: A setter grumbles that sticking at a mindless, boring task is their work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'me' is the setter, whose job is writing clues. 'soulless' cuts the middle S from USE, leaving UE.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing the hints for a crossword is the work of its setter, who speaks as 'me'.

clue.text: Engraving art by the medium of dog dirt: "retro"!

definitions.note: plural answer for a singular art; the carvings stand for the craft

parts.note: in, as in written in ink
to tag along is to dog, follow someone

indicators.note: backward-looking, so the word is turned round

parts.note: soil is earth, dirt

explanation.surface: A mock-art piece engraved using dog mess, in a retro style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retro' turns SOIL into LIOS.
explanation.definitionFit: These are designs cut into the surface of a gem or plate, the reverse of a cameo, examples of incised carving.

clue.text: Free ASTATINE?

parts.note: the element astatine has symbol At, and the word is printed in capitals, so its symbol is shown in big type

explanation.surface: A puzzled call to release the element.
explanation.walkthrough: The element printed in capitals is its symbol At set in large type.
explanation.definitionFit: A criminal who is free and not yet caught is said to be on the loose, an idiom with the same meaning.

clue.text: Clashers on stand one has reduced in height

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the letters for height

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the word is cut short by its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone's cymbals on a stand have been lowered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' cuts HAS to HA.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum kit's pedal-operated pair of cymbals on a stand, which clash together.

clue.text: Knit top for the wife between 1300 and 2100 hours?

parts.note: 1300 hours is one o'clock in the afternoon, so I, Roman one

indicators.note: the letters go in the middle of the two times

parts.note: 2100 hours is nine o'clock in the evening

indicators.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A wife knits a sweater between lunchtime and the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: On a 12-hour clock 1300 is one and 2100 is nine, giving I and NINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to interlace or twist together, which is what this variant spelling of a verb means.

clue.text: This played in earnest without lawn originally?

definitions.text: This played in earnest without lawn originally?

indicators.note: old sense of outside, wrapped around the other letter
the letters are played about with and rearranged
only the first letter of lawn is used

explanation.surface: A game taken seriously and not played on grass.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of IN EARNEST goes around L. 'without' means outside; real tennis, the indoor court game, predates lawn tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: The original indoor court game is played seriously and never on grass, unlike its later lawn offspring.

clue.text: Fibre ____, making sign align

parts.note: put AL where the S of the first word stands and it becomes the second

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank about a fibre that straightens a sign.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is filled by an instruction: S IS AL, so the S of 'sign' becomes AL and it reads 'align'.
explanation.definitionFit: This stiff plant fibre from an agave is used for rope and matting.

clue.text: Initiate utility room's sequence

indicators.note: a run of consecutive letters taken out of the phrase

explanation.surface: Start up the utility room's programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initiate' looks like a verb but is a noun, a beginner.
explanation.definitionFit: A newcomer just initiated into a field is a beginner or novice, a synonym.

clue.text: Capital invested in adjoining abattoirs?

parts.note: set two copies of the slaughterhouse word side by side, and a North African capital lies across the point where they join

explanation.surface: Money put into abattoirs next door to each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money but is a city. Set two abattoirs end to end and the run spans the join: abattoiR ABATtoir.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the capital of Morocco, so it is a capital in the sense of a seat of government.

clue.text: They're high-calibre doubles, with King dominating bill

definitions.note: plural, guns described by their bore

indicators.note: the king takes over the place of the bill

parts.note: dead ringers are exact lookalikes, doubles
an ad is an advertisement, a bill or poster
R is for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: First-class lookalikes, with the king ruling the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap AD for R in DEAD RINGERS. 'high-calibre' looks like praise but refers to bore size.
explanation.definitionFit: These small pocket pistols fire a large-bore bullet, hence high in calibre.

clue.text: Last of The Arsenal Years?

indicators.note: the final letter of the word

parts.note: the Royal Artillery, RA, is a gunners' regiment; Arsenal FC are the Gunners

explanation.surface: The final seasons of Arsenal, the London football club.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal Football Club is nicknamed the Gunners, linking it to the Royal Artillery, RA.
explanation.definitionFit: A long period of time, an age or epoch, can be stood in for by a span of years.

clue.text: The ultimate in culture? Let me think about Hull's character

indicators.note: the very last letter of the word
turned about, so read the other way

parts.note: um is a hesitant sound while thinking

explanation.surface: Musing on what counts as the height of culture, in a famous puppet act.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod Hull was a British entertainer whose aggressive bird puppet was his character; 'Hull' looks like the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Rod Hull's notorious puppet was a large flightless Australian bird, his on-screen character.

clue.text: Literary code survives note on reverse

parts.note: is, in the sense of exists or lives on

indicators.note: the note letters are turned round

parts.note: NB, nota bene, is a note to take notice

explanation.surface: A literary code is still there, written as a note on the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reverse' looks like the back of a page but turns NB into BN.
explanation.definitionFit: The International Standard Book Number identifies a book, a code used in publishing.

clue.text: In which Indy you'd find Jumbo GK crossword with no empty spaces?

definitions.text: In which Indy you'd find Jumbo GK crossword
definitions.meaning: split as ..., the Saturday edition of the Independent, which ran the large general-knowledge puzzle

explanation.surface: Which issue of the Independent runs the big general-knowledge puzzle that leaves no blanks?
explanation.walkthrough: Indy is the Independent newspaper; its jumbo general-knowledge crossword ran on Saturdays.
explanation.definitionFit: Being full up after a meal means having no room left, so it describes something filled completely.

clue.text: You and I quickly wanting to be let out from it?

definitions.text: You and I quickly wanting to be let out from it?

indicators.note: the letters are put out of order

parts.note: quickly written, as in a text message, you is U and I stays I

explanation.surface: Two people trapped somewhere desperately want to be released.
explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: U and I with TO BE LET, shuffled; the whole clue describes the dungeon.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret dungeon with an opening only at the top, from which prisoners would naturally want release.
